[David Bernard] Welcome to the SubClub Podcast, a show dedicated to the best practices for building and growing app businesses. We sit down with the entrepreneurs, investors, and builders behind the most successful apps in the world, to learn from their successes and failures. SubClub is brought to you by Revenue Cat. Let's get into the show. Hello, I'm your host, David Bernard. My guest today is Jake Castillo, co-founder of CalAI, the AI calorie tracker with over 15 million downloads, now a part of MyFitnessPal. On the podcast, I talk with Jake about the magic moment test for whether creators can sell your app, the one number that caps what you can pay them, and why cloning hit apps like CalAI rarely pays off. Hey Jake, thanks so much for joining me on the podcast today.

[Jake Castillo] Yeah, it's really crazy to think about because there is so much luck involved and so many fortunate wins for me that happened along the way that needed to happen in order for this whole journey to have occurred. And then from 8 to like 2 a.m. every day, I would work on Oliver's project at StudyBuddy. And then if you would, kind of relate it to what your advice would be today, and if you think things are different today or if you think people should kind of rerun that same playbook.

[Jake Castillo] Our thesis stemmed from the fact that we were a calorie tracker, and we felt that the people that track their calories the most were people that were in health and fitness. And then when we looked in the health and fitness space, we saw that there's millions and millions of creators. There's probably more health and fitness creators than any other creator niche out there, right? So there's all of these creators, but there's a finite number of brands available to these creators. You've got protein powders, you've got athleisure wear. That's about it, right? And they can only work with so many creators. So there was all of these creators that never had had a brand deal before. And we finally gave them an opportunity to get a brand deal. So that was like the first, there was just a huge supply, the well-ran deep. And then on top of that, the content that these creators were making made it super easy to integrate CalAI into those videos. These creators were already making "What I Eat in a Day" videos. There's a million other creators doing the same types of content, the same type of content as Dawson. So let's just copy and paste." We did that, and it worked tremendously well. As for should this be the playbook for apps moving forward in today's environment, I think if all of those variables ring true for your app, then absolutely, right? Now, that's not the case, right? If you're an astrology app, there's not millions of creators out there. And what are the brands available to astrology creators? Probably other astrology apps, right? That's kind of it. And those apps, if they got their stuff buttoned up, they've probably already signed those creators to exclusivity deals, which can make it tricky. So it's just like, yeah, you got to suss out the environment.

[Jake Castillo] And nothing. And we couldn't figure out why. The last thing they want to think about is tracking their calories because that's just going to give them bad news, right? [David Bernard] Any other specific tactics or tips or strategies to figure out which creator niches, which types of content work and don't work?

[Jake Castillo] Yeah. I mean, so I think the main thing people need to understand is views can lie, followers can lie, but comments cannot, right? The truth is always in the comments. And in a couple different ways. First and foremost, if you want to understand, is this niche relevant to my app? Look in the comment section of the big creators in that space. And are people looking for a solution that your app solves? If so, that's prime time. You go full steam ahead. And then additionally, on a more granular level, if you're trying to identify whether or not an individual creator, you already identified that the niche is going to work and the content type works, but it's like, will this actual creator work? Because for every 10 creators out there, 9 of them probably won't convert and only 1 will. So how do you find out which is the 1 out of 9, 1 out of 10? The way you do that is in the comment section and you look. I put it on two different sides. You've got one comment section, let's say it's a girl going through leg day, right? And it's her workout routine. And if you go look at on health and fitness pages right now, you'll find a bunch of creators like this with comment sections like this, where the comment is a bunch of guys and it's like fire emoji, fire emoji, fire emoji, or the emoji where the guy's sweating and that stuff. So there's that type of comment section. And then there's another type of comment section where it's like, "Thank you so much for posting this video. I was really unsure of how to work out my hamstrings or quads or glutes. And this video gave me the info necessary." One of those comment sections is going to convert, one of them is not. And I think it's pretty obvious which one will.

[David Bernard] That's such a great insight too. I mean, and these are the things. You think, "Oh, female creator, she's good-looking, she gets a ton of views," but then you got to introspect. Why is she getting those views? What kind of people are watching? Why are they watching? And unfortunately for some of those, it's not what you would think. And it's not the other women excited to try that next workout, so.

[David Bernard] Yeah. How do you think about pricing that? How do you structure your deals? So when he's doing 10,000-view posts and then all of a sudden one pops off, were you on the hook for a ton of money? How did you structure that?

[Jake Castillo] Yeah. So this is a key thing I think all founders should keep in mind is with influencer and UGC content, you are banking on a the real money is made in the viral hits, right? You base your break-even point or profitable rate on their average views. And it's like, "Okay, this is the most likely scenario. We'll break even, maybe get a little profit." And where you make your real money is when they have one video go mega viral and all that is profit. And if you're not doing flat rates, it makes it hard to capture that asymmetric upside that is a viral hit. So whenever possible, I would try to do flat-rate deals because it allows you to capture the asymmetry that is algorithmic content.

For those who listen to the podcast and livestreams regularly, I vibe-coded a little app. I didn't expect it to make a bunch of money or anything.
